name: Bianca Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Totally fine. I like talking about this, my partner's sick of hearing about it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior at Greenline Energy, a small installer with eight of us, doing solar panels, heat pump wiring and car chargers on houses and farm shops. I'm usually on a roof or in a loft running cable to the inverter, which is the box that turns solar power into normal household power. I photograph every fuse board and ask an AI app to explain anything I don't understand, then I check with Owen, the lead electrician. The roofs in winter are brutal, and I'm still slow at fault-finding, but I genuinely love the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold but still useful, because it is for me. I'd post something like, it didn't change the world but it got me through my exams. At work I'd tease Owen, who never trusted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never the thing that worried me. My firm lives on the government's solar grant, not on AI. If that grant gets cut, I'm out of work long before any robot shows up. I've got about 350 saved since my car's clutch went, which is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI app to revise for my licence exam every night on the bus home. I'd ask Owen if I can do a few weekend battery jobs for extra hours. I'd write to my local politician about keeping the solar grant, because that's my actual job security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not about tech. I'd feel fine about my skills and nervous about the grant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the grant does go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Greenline would lose maybe half its jobs overnight, because most of our customers only go solar with the grant. Owen and the senior lads would stay, and I'd be first out the door. Then it's three other firms in the area, and none of them do green work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ravi, your partner, think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi drives a bus, so he thinks I'm obsessed. He'd say, see, nothing happened, now stop reading about it at dinner. He's probably right in this picture.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold** but still **useful** to me.
I'd post that AI got me through my **exams**, even if it changed little else.
think: My real risk is the government's **solar grant**, not AI.
With about **350 saved** after a car repair, I can't ride out a slow spell.
do: Revise for my **licence exam** with the AI app on the bus home.
Ask Owen for **weekend battery jobs** for extra hours.
Write to my local politician to **keep the solar grant**.
feel: Uneasy about the **grant**, confident about my growing **skills**.
S0.quote: My firm lives on the government's solar grant, not on AI. If that grant gets cut, I'm out of work long before any robot shows up.
fieldNote: She is an **eager AI user** who doesn't see AI as her threat here.
Her job depends on a **government grant**, a political risk she watches closely.
Her partner's teasing shows the **gap** between her interest and his.

steps.text: Revise for the licence exam with the AI app each night
Take weekend battery jobs from Owen for extra pay
Write to her local politician about keeping the solar grant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, this one I like. Quotes, booking, ordering, that's the stuff that slows us down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be brilliant for green trades if the gains are shared. I'd post that we could fit twice the solar with the same people. I'd also say the office staff need retraining, not the sack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. An AI that drafts every quote overnight means my firm can book twice the roofs. Twice the roofs needs twice the hands, and I've got hands. The worry is Linda, who does our bookings, because her whole job is on that list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the design tools that plan solar layouts, so I can do surveys as well as wiring. I'd sign up for the battery storage course in spring, which costs about 300, paid monthly. I'd show Owen how to use the quoting app, because he'd never do it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, and a little guilty about Linda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the course costs 300. Where does that come from with 350 saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Monthly payments, 25 a month, and I'd skip buying a new phone. If I wait until I can afford things, I'll never do anything. My mum thinks that's reckless, I think it's how you get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your own work that this picture touches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fault-finding, maybe, because AI would get good at telling you which circuit's the problem. That's my weak spot, so it would help me. The roof and the cable and the drill are still all mine.

say: I'd say this could be **brilliant for green trades** if gains are shared.
I'd argue office staff need **retraining**, not the sack.
think: AI quoting lets Greenline book **more roofs**, which needs more hands like mine.
Linda's **bookings job** is on the list, which worries me.
do: Learn the **solar design tools** so I can do surveys too.
Start the **battery storage course** in spring at 25 a month.
feel: Excited, with some **guilt** about Linda's job.
S1.quote: An AI that drafts every quote overnight means my firm can book twice the roofs. Twice the roofs needs twice the hands, and I've got hands.
fieldNote: She sees **thinking AI** as a boost for a hands-on green installer.
She pays for training on **monthly payments** despite thin savings.
Her concern turns to a **colleague**, not herself.

steps.text: Learn the solar layout design tool to do site surveys
Pay 25 a month for the battery storage course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, five for the robots. That's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a public plan for workers, like a green transition fund but bigger. I'd join anything organised by the renewables workers' network. I'd post a lot, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd have a great three years and then a hard landing. Thinking AI could make me a great electrician by 2028, just in time for robots to make great electricians cheap in 2031. And Ravi's bus job could go even sooner, because driving is mostly an AI problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend 2027 learning to commission and test automated systems, because someone has to set up the robots. I'd move from 25 to 60 a week into savings and sell my car if Ravi still has the bus pass. I'd join the network's push for a transition fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Thrilled for one year and frightened about the fifth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture the night you and Ravi talk about it. What's said?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can't both be in jobs a machine can do by 2031, so one of us has to move first. Ravi would say it's me, because I like this stuff. He'd be right, but it's a lot to carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell your car. How would you get to roofs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In Greenline's van, I'd pick it up from Owen's yard. It adds an hour to my day, but the car costs me 200 a month. It's the obvious first cut.

say: I'd call for a **public transition fund** for workers.
I'd join the **renewables workers' network** and post about it.
think: Thinking AI makes me a better electrician just before robots arrive in **2031**.
Ravi's **bus job** could go even sooner, because driving is mostly AI.
do: Learn to **commission and test** automated systems through 2027.
Raise savings to **60 a week** and sell my car.
Join the network's push for a **transition fund**.
feel: Anxious: **thrilled** for a year, **frightened** about the fifth.
S2.quote: Thinking AI could make me a great electrician by 2028, just in time for robots to make great electricians cheap in 2031.
fieldNote: She spots the **irony**: AI lifts her skills just before robots cheapen them.
Her partner's **bus job** adds household risk before hers.
She accepts being the **one who moves first**, but feels its weight.

steps.text: Train to commission and test automated equipment during 2027
Sell the car and save 60 a week
Join the renewables workers' network campaign for a transition fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 and 2034. Okay. Five years is enough to make a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should train people now for jobs alongside robots. I'd post that every apprentice should learn to work with automation. I'd make a fuss at the network about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in a decent spot if I use the time. With five years, I'd stop being the junior who uses AI and become the person who sets up the robots on solar jobs. Somebody has to bolt the panels where the robot can't reach and sign off the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my licence in 2027, then the battery course, then look for a robotics commissioning course with a solar firm. I'd save 40 a week. Ravi and I would talk about him training as a bus mechanic, because buses still need fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in a hopeful way. Like the start of a hard climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ravi could train as a mechanic. Has that come up before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi has said he wants out of driving anyway, because of his back. So this picture just pushes it forward. I'd find him the course, because he wouldn't look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robots get good at roofs faster than you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be in the van fixing robots instead of fitting panels. I'd rather that than be in an office. Either way I'd want to be the one who understands them.

say: I'd say every apprentice should learn to **work with automation**.
I'd push the network to **train people now**.
think: Five years lets me become the person who **sets up robots** on solar jobs.
Someone still has to **sign off** the system and work where robots can't reach.
do: Finish my **licence** in 2027, then the battery course.
Find a **robotics commissioning** course with a solar firm.
Save **40** a week and help Ravi into **bus mechanics**.
feel: Anxious but **hopeful**, like the start of a hard climb.
S3.quote: With five years, I'd stop being the junior who uses AI and become the person who sets up the robots on solar jobs.
fieldNote: She frames five years as time to **change roles**, not leave the trade.
She plans for **Ravi's career** too, not just her own.
She'd rather **fix robots** than retreat to office work.

steps.text: Finish the licence in 2027 and then the battery course
Enrol in a robotics commissioning course with a solar firm
Find Ravi a bus mechanic training course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for robots. I'd be pushing 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty if governments start now, so no more excuses. I'd say green trades are the best bet for young people. I'd keep posting about it, Ravi would keep sighing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the dream version. Ten years is enough time to get a licence, a van and my own small firm, and still have a few good years before robots catch up. I'd want to own something by then, not just be on someone's payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get licensed, work two more years at Greenline, then start a small solar and battery firm around 2031 with a used van. I'd use AI for quotes and bookings from day one so I don't need an office. I'd still back a public plan for workers who can't do what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good about my own chances, uneasy for everyone in the trade who doesn't like computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the money for a van and a firm come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving 40 a week for four years gets me most of the way to a used van. The rest would be a small business loan. It's scary on my income, but I'd rather try than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned people who don't like computers. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen, honestly. He's the best electrician I know and he won't touch an app. In ten years he'd be near retirement, but the lads like him who are 40 now are the ones I'd worry about.

say: I'd say a **decade is plenty** if governments start now.
I'd tell young people **green trades** are the best bet.
think: Ten years gives me time for a **licence, a van** and my own firm.
I'd want to **own something** before robots arrive.
do: Get licensed and work **two more years** at Greenline.
Start a small **solar and battery firm** around 2031 with a used van.
Run quotes and bookings with **AI** from day one.
feel: Uneasy: good about my chances, worried for colleagues who **avoid computers**.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to get a licence, a van and my own small firm, and still have a few good years before robots catch up.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her into a would-be **business owner**.
Her plan relies on **steady saving** and a small loan on low pay.
Her worry moves to **older colleagues** who avoid technology.

steps.text: Get the electrician's licence and stay two years at Greenline
Start a small solar and battery firm with a used van
Use AI for quotes and bookings instead of an office
Back a public plan for workers who can't retrain

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ravi and I would both be exposed within a few years and we have no cushion. What would help is a paid transition fund, so I could train in robotics without skipping rent. I'm the one telling everyone at work to try AI, and I'm also the one who'd lose my job to it first. Both are true.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the grant. People think the threat to a solar electrician is AI, but it's politics and subsidies. One budget decision could end my job faster than any robot.

headlineQuote: I'm the one telling everyone at work to try AI, and I'm also the one who'd lose my job to it first. Both are true.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old junior** at a small solar and heat pump installer.
She uses AI **every day** to learn, revise and understand fuse boards.
In calm pictures, her real threat is the **solar grant**, not technology.
Fast AGI worries her because partner Ravi's **bus job** and her roof work both go.
Given time, she plans a licence, **robotics training** and her own small firm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Ravi would both be exposed with no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid transition fund** so she can train in robotics without missing rent.
